implementation_notes: The command half is an `ICommand`/abstract `CommandBase` with a single Execute(); the codec is the BCL. System.Text.Json with [JsonPolymorphic] and one [JsonDerivedType] per command writes the discriminator and will only ever instantiate types explicitly opted in, which is the safe default for a queue other producers can reach. The worker deserialises the envelope, resolves the derived type and calls Execute; the queue (MSMQ, Azure Queue/Service Bus, RabbitMQ) supplies durability and retries.
pitfalls: Polymorphic configuration is not inherited: each level of the hierarchy needs its own [JsonDerivedType] list, and an unknown discriminator throws unless UnknownDerivedTypeHandling is set - which must not silently fall back on a queue you do not control.
Init-only and required members round-trip differently from the default-constructor shape that legacy serialisers expected; verify the codec against messages already sitting in the queue.
Discriminator strings are the wire contract: renaming a type or changing the property name invalidates in-flight commands unless the old name is kept as an alias.

variants.name: Legacy [Serializable] command over System.Messaging/MSMQ (historic form)
variants.implementation_notes: This is the shape the pattern was popularised with on .NET: commands implement a common interface or base class, carry a [Serializable] attribute plus a default constructor so the formatter can rebuild them, and travel through System.Messaging.MessageQueue with the binary formatter; the invoker reads the message body and calls Execute. It is listed as a variant only for maintaining existing systems: BinaryFormatter is removed in .NET 9 and unconstrained polymorphic deserialization was a documented remote-code-execution vector, so new designs must use System.Text.Json or a schema-driven codec.
pitfalls: BinaryFormatter on a queue with any untrusted producer is equivalent to remote code execution; keep it behind an authenticated, single-producer broker, or migrate the payload to a schema-driven codec.
BinaryFormatter is removed in .NET 9, so this variant pins the worker to .NET Framework or to an earlier runtime with the obsolete feature switched on.
Serialised field order and assembly-qualified type names are the contract: moving a type to another assembly or reordering fields breaks old messages.
